terms.gloss: a consul, one of the two chief magistrates of Rome
terms.comment: Two were elected each year after the kings were driven out (Lewis & Short), and the year was named after them. The consulship is cōnsulātus (Traupman 179). A modern consul is another office altogether (see consul, a state’s representative abroad); Levi and Bini note that the two share only the name (p. 51).

terms.gloss: of a consul, consular; as a noun, a man who has been consul
terms.comment: Comitia cōnsulāria, the election of consuls; homō or vir cōnsulāris, an ex-consul (Cicero).

phrases.latin: ita Canīniō cōnsule scītō nēminem prandisse
phrases.english: so, I’ll have you know, while Caninius was consul nobody had lunch (he held office for one afternoon)

sources: Enrico Levi and Arturo Bini, Il latino come lingua viva (1937), p. 51, s.v. pretore.
Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-cicero-epistulae), checked against the editions named there.
